beats.say: Start with the thing everyone talks about and almost nobody has looked inside. A trained model is a file.
Open it, and there is nothing else in there. No rules, no instructions, no text. Just a very long list of numbers, each one somewhere between about minus one and plus one.
beats.show: file opens into a grid of weight tiles with numbers, cascading in

beats.say: Forty are drawn here. A large model has seventy billion of them.
Each number is called a parameter, or a weight. The two words mean the same thing.
beats.show: one tile lifts out with label weight = parameter

beats.say: Here is where thirty milliseconds comes from. Time per token is the bytes you must read, divided by how many bytes the chip can read each second.
A hundred and forty gigabytes of weights. On an H one hundred, at three point three five terabytes per second, that is forty-one point eight milliseconds per token.
On an H two hundred, at four point eight terabytes per second, twenty-nine point two. On a B two hundred, at eight, seventeen point five.
The middle row lands on twenty-nine milliseconds, which is where the round figure of thirty comes from. It is not a guess. It is a division.
Here is the chip, and here is the memory beside it. Every weight lives over here, in the memory, and the arithmetic happens over there, on the chip.
So for every token, all one hundred and forty gigabytes have to cross this bus, from the memory into the chip. Every single time.
Zoom in, and the arithmetic units are mostly waiting. Put the two numbers on one chart and the reason becomes a picture.
Decode sits at one operation per byte, far to the left of the ridge at two hundred and ninety-five. It can only go as fast as the memory lets it.
The model predicts one token, adds it to the text, and runs again, round and round.
Reading a hundred and forty gigabytes takes twenty seconds from a disk, and forty-two milliseconds from the memory beside the chip.
A specification sheet has four lines, and only one of them is an amount.
